newsitem.title: SPAIN: Spain bourse expected to toast winery offerings.
newsitem.headline: Spain bourse expected to toast winery offerings.

text.p: Three years of top-flight grape harvests and a booming bourse are likely to ensure the success of the share offerings of two producers of Spanish Rioja wine, analysts and dealers said on Thursday.
Two of the region's most respected names -- Compania Vinicola del Norte de Espana (CVNE) and Baron de Ley -- announced on Wednesday their intention to list on the bourse.
CVNE, which produces the brands CUNE, Imperial and Vina Real, is planning a public share offering and a capital rise. Baron de Ley will sell up to 74.6 percent of its share capital.
"The placements are small. There is an appetite for paper from new companies. They won't have any trouble placing it," said Juan Cueto, chief analyst at Ibersecurities.

For the region, the heart of Spanish wine production, the last three grape harvests have been among the century's best, particularly 1994 and 1995, with ample and top-quality yields. This year's harvest is also expected to be good.
These yields, and the resulting boost to profits, should combine with the dramatic recent run of the bourse to draw in investors, analysts said.
"There is a lot of demand...for small groups that can revalue," said an analyst at a Spanish brokerage.
At its peak, hit on May 28, the IBEX index of 35 leading shares had risen more than 30 percent in 1997.

Investors hungrily snapped up the bourse's two giant privatisations of the year, Telefonica de Espana and Repsol, as well as the flotation of fashion house Adolfo Dominguez -- the only other offerings this year.
But the two wine growers have yet to give details of the offer, and analysts caution that the group may have trouble maintaining profit levels should future harvests drop in quality.

"This is a business with a certain amount of cyclicity. They have had some very good years and this one will be good as well. But one could have doubts about the sustainability of profits," said Ibersecurities' Cueto.
So far, CVNE, which was founded in 1879 by the grandfather of the current chairman, has simply said it intends to take steps for a public share offering and a capital rise.

Baron de Ley, with a capital base of 4.85 billion pesetas ($33.2 million), said its share sale would be directed at institutional investors, domestic and international investment funds, pension funds and portfolio managers. There will be no retail tranche.
"It's a little bit early to tell (the success of the sale). It's a growing market and people are underweight...But it's hard to forecast future harvests," a dealer said.
Currently, there is only one other winery traded on the Madrid bourse, Bodegas y Bebidas. Beermaker El Alguila, a unit of Heineken, is also listed.
"There is a sector just of wine growers being formed," one analyst said.
